prime.problem: Quantization promises 2× or 4× from fewer bits, but a serving step reads weights, reads KV and does math, and each format shrinks different parts. Pick the wrong one for your batch size and you get almost nothing: 4-bit weights can make chat decode 3.7× faster and a full-batch server 1.04× faster.
prime.fits: The 'fewer bytes per step' lever. It uses course 2's step formula and critical batch size, and course 3's tensor-core formats, and asks which format helps which regime.
expect: W8A8 (SmoothQuant) and FP8: weights and activations
the regime map: decode at small vs large batch, prefill
prime.goal: Predict which format speeds up decode at batch 1, decode at full batch and prefill, and explain why real gains fall short of the bit ratio.

attend: Which term of the step formula does W4A16 shrink, and why does its math still run at the BF16 rate?
Why does W4A16's advantage fade once the batch passes about 76, while W8A8 keeps its prefill gain?
What in the KV cache does neither weight format touch, and how large is it at batch 238?
Why are activations harder to quantize than weights, and how does SmoothQuant move the difficulty?
What three changes let GPTQ scale OBQ-style error compensation to 175B parameters?

must: W4A16 stores weights in 4 bits but unpacks them to BF16 before the multiply → the weight read shrinks ×0.26 but math runs at 989 TFLOPS → decode at small batch (bytes-bound) gets 3.70× → prefill (math-bound) gets 1.00× → the MLP's B_crit drops to 76, past which the math sets the step
W8A8/FP8 quantizes activations too → the matmul runs on 8-bit tensor cores at 2× rate and weights are ×0.5 → prefill 2.00×, batch-1 decode 1.97×, and it wins from B = 148 up
Neither format shrinks the KV reads → at B = 238 they're 19.07 of 23.86 ms (80%) → full-batch gains collapse to 1.04–1.11× → KV quantization is the lever for that part

Activation outliers ~100× larger sit in fixed channels → one INT8 scale leaves normal channels 2–3 levels → divide activations by s and multiply weights by s (an exact identity) → both become quantizable, with α splitting the difficulty
elevated: INT8 GEMM kernels can apply scales only along tokens and output channels, after the multiply → per-input-channel activation scales are impossible there → which is why smoothing folds the scale into the previous layer offline
W4A16 dequantizes inside the main loop (3 extra ops per weight, per AWQ), W8A8 in the epilogue → part of why real gains fall short of the bit ratio
reference: GPTQ's Hessian, lazy batch size 128 and 1% dampening
AWQ's grid search over α and group size 128
Kiely's sensitivity ranking and page numbers

compress.prompt: Draw the step formula from memory and mark, with arrows, which term each format shrinks. Then sketch the speedup-vs-batch curve for W4A16 and W8A8 (log B), marking B = 76, B = 148 and B = 238.
checklist: weight read: both shrink it; math: only W8A8/FP8 speeds it up; KV reads: neither
W4A16: 3.70× at B = 1, fades after B = 76, 1.04× at 238, 1.00× prefill
W8A8: 1.97× at B = 1, 2.00× prefill, 1.11× at 238, ahead from B = 148
real gains leak through KV, dequant overhead and high-precision ops: 30–50%
SmoothQuant moves outlier difficulty from activations to weights with an exact rescaling

retrieve.q: Explain why 4-bit weight-only quantization speeds up chat decode but not a long-prompt prefill.
answer: prefill of 1,000 tokens is 16.1 TFLOP of math, 16.24 ms at 989 TFLOPS; the 4.79 or 1.24 ms weight read hides under it
W4A16 unpacks weights to BF16, so the math rate doesn't change
batch-1 decode is 0.02 ms of math and 4.79 ms of weight reads, so shrinking bytes is nearly the whole win

retrieve.q: Walk through SmoothQuant's transformation for one linear layer: what is divided, what is multiplied, where the division goes at run time, and what α controls.
answer: Y = (X diag(s)⁻¹)(diag(s) W): exactly the same product
activation channel j is divided by s_j, weight row j multiplied by s_j
the division folds into the previous layer offline, so it costs nothing at run time
s_j = max|X_j|^α ÷ max|W_j|^(1−α): α = 0 leaves outliers in X, 1 moves them all into W

retrieve.q: You serve Llama-3.1-8B on an H100 for a busy API at full batch, and separately on an A100 for a single user. Which format do you choose for each, and why not the same one?
answer: H100 full batch: FP8 W8A8, since it's the only format that also helps math-bound prefill and large batch (1.11× at 238, 2.00× prefill)
A100 single user: W4A16 (GPTQ/AWQ), since batch-1 decode is bytes-bound and the A100 has no FP8 tensor cores
at full batch neither weight format helps much; KV quantization or fewer KV heads is the bigger lever

compare.q: Weight quantization and KV-cache quantization shrink different bytes. At batch 1 and at batch 238, which one matters more on the running example, and how does each fail on quality?
answer: batch 1: weights dominate (4.79 of 4.87 ms), so weight quantization matters
batch 238: KV reads are 80% of the step, so KV quantization matters
weights are the least sensitive to quantization; KV errors compound token to token (Kiely's ranking)

compare.q: Quantization and speculative decoding both speed up small-batch decode. What is fundamentally different about how they do it, and how does each one's gain change as batch grows?
answer: quantization makes each step read fewer bytes; speculation gets more tokens out of each weight read
quantization's gain fades as KV reads dominate but never goes below 1× in our model
speculation's gain disappears once the step turns compute-bound, and can go below 1× (0.70× at B = 256 in course 2's model)

predict.q: Move from 2k to 8k context at the largest batch that fits in BF16 (59 sequences). Do W4A16's and FP8's full-batch gains grow or shrink compared with 2k, and why? Commit to a direction for each.
predict.answer: Our recomputation: at B = 59 and 8k, BF16 is 23.70 ms, W4A16 20.15 ms (1.18×), FP8 21.31 ms (1.11×). W4A16's full-batch gain grows compared with 2k's 1.04×: only 59–70 sequences fit, which is below its B_crit of 76, so its step is still bound by bytes rather than BF16 math. At each format's own maximum batch the lab gives +19% for W4A16 and +13% for W8A8 (2k: +4% and +13%). But KV is still about 80% of the step (18.9 of 23.7 ms), so neither comes near batch 1's 3.70× or 1.97×.

apply.task: Using the card's step formula (KV reads + max(math at the format's rate, weight read)), compute the BF16, W4A16 and FP8 step at 8k context for B = 1 and B = 59. Report each speedup vs BF16 and the share of the BF16 step that is KV reads at B = 59. Then say in one sentence which lever would help the B = 59 case most.
apply.done: Six step times with four speedups, a KV share in %, and a one-sentence lever choice, before checking.
apply.hint: Check after trying (our recomputation): B = 1: BF16 5.12 ms, W4A16 1.56 ms (3.29×), FP8 2.72 ms (1.88×). B = 59: BF16 23.70, W4A16 20.15 (1.18×), FP8 21.31 (1.11×). KV reads ≈ 79.8% of the BF16 step, so quantize the KV cache (course 4).
